_link.title: I can compare the Maxwell-Boltzmann representations of a temperature increase and a catalyst on the same diagram

toLevel2.stem: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram, a temperature increase is shown by:
toLevel2.answer: shifting the distribution curve to the right
distractors: moving the Ea line to the left
making the curve taller and narrower
removing the Ea line from the diagram

toLevel2.stem: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram, adding a catalyst is shown by:
toLevel2.answer: moving the Ea marker to the left
distractors: shifting the curve to the right
making the curve shorter and broader
increasing the area under the curve

toLevel2.stem: When comparing temperature and catalyst effects on the same Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram, which element changes for a temperature increase?
distractors: The Ea marker position
The total area under the curve
The x-axis label

toLevel2.stem: When comparing temperature and catalyst effects on the same diagram, which element changes for a catalyst?
distractors: The distribution curve shape
The total area under the curve
The y-axis scale

toLevel2.stem: Both a temperature increase and a catalyst result in:
toLevel2.answer: a larger proportion of particles able to react
distractors: a smaller proportion of particles able to react
a change in the total number of particles
a decrease in the rate of reaction

toLevel2.stem: A temperature increase shifts the distribution curve to the right, while a catalyst shifts the Ea marker to the left.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: Both a temperature increase and a catalyst change the shape of the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: A temperature increase shifts the {{blank:1}} to the right, while a catalyst shifts the {{blank:2}} to the left.
distractors: Ea marker
curve
peak
x-axis

toLevel2.stem: On a combined diagram, the area between the uncatalysed and catalysed Ea markers represents the {{blank:1}} particles that can react only when a {{blank:2}} is present.
distractors: fewer
solvent
original
reactant

toLevel2.stem: Both a temperature increase and a catalyst increase the {{blank:1}} of particles able to react, but they achieve this by changing different {{blank:2}} on the diagram.
distractors: number
axes
mass
labels

toLevel3.stem: Why does a temperature increase change the curve shape but not the Ea position?
toLevel3.answer: Temperature changes particle energies but the reaction's energy barrier stays the same
distractors: Temperature always changes both the curve and the Ea position simultaneously
Temperature lowers the Ea so the marker must move to the left as well
Temperature has no effect on the Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram at all

toLevel3.stem: Why does a catalyst change the Ea position but not the curve shape?
toLevel3.answer: A catalyst lowers the energy threshold without changing particle energies or temperature
distractors: A catalyst gives particles more energy, which should change the curve
A catalyst changes both the curve and the Ea but only the Ea is noticeable
A catalyst increases temperature, but this is not shown on the diagram

toLevel3.stem: On a combined diagram, why is the shaded area beyond Ea larger for both a catalysed reaction and a higher-temperature reaction?
toLevel3.answer: Both effects increase the proportion of particles with enough energy to react
distractors: Both effects create new particles that did not exist before
Both effects reduce the total area under the curve equally
Both effects shift the curve to the left on the diagram

toLevel3.stem: How can you distinguish between the effect of a catalyst and a temperature increase on the same Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram?
toLevel3.answer: A catalyst moves the Ea line; a temperature increase changes the curve shape
distractors: Both effects look identical and cannot be distinguished on the same diagram
A catalyst changes the curve shape; a temperature increase moves the Ea line
A catalyst increases the area under the curve; temperature decreases it

toLevel3.stem: Why does being able to compare both effects on a single diagram demonstrate thorough understanding?
toLevel3.answer: It shows the student can identify which diagram feature corresponds to each mechanism
distractors: It proves the student can calculate the exact activation energy value
It shows the student can draw a perfect Maxwell-Boltzmann curve freehand
It demonstrates that both effects are identical and interchangeable

toLevel3.stem: On a diagram showing both effects, a student notices that the higher-temperature curve extends further to the right. What does this indicate?
toLevel3.answer: More particles have very high kinetic energies at the higher temperature
distractors: The catalyst has increased the kinetic energy of all particles
The activation energy has increased due to the temperature change
The total number of particles has increased at higher temperature

toLevel3.stem: On a combined diagram, a catalyst changes the Ea marker position while the distribution curve stays the same, whereas a temperature increase changes the curve while Ea stays fixed.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: A catalyst changes the {{blank:1}} on the diagram, while a temperature increase changes the {{blank:2}} — this is how the two effects are distinguished.
distractors: curve shape
Ea position
total area
x-axis

toLevel3.stem: Both effects increase the shaded area beyond the Ea line, meaning a greater {{blank:1}} of particles have sufficient energy to {{blank:2}}.
distractors: number
collide
mass
dissolve

toLevel3.stem: The higher-temperature curve extends further to the {{blank:1}}, showing that more particles have very {{blank:2}} kinetic energies.
distractors: left
low
centre
average

toLevel4.stem: A student is asked to draw a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram showing both a temperature increase and a catalyst effect. What should appear on the diagram?
toLevel4.answer: Two curves (original and higher-temperature) and two Ea lines (uncatalysed and catalysed)
distractors: One curve and one Ea line showing both effects combined
Two curves only, with no Ea lines shown on the diagram
Two Ea lines only, with no curves shown on the diagram

toLevel4.stem: On a combined diagram, a student shades the area between the two Ea lines under the original curve. What does this shaded area represent?
toLevel4.answer: Particles that can react with the catalyst but not without it
distractors: Particles that can react at higher temperature but not at lower temperature
Particles that cannot react under any circumstances at all
The total energy released by the catalysed reaction pathway

toLevel4.stem: A student needs to show on one diagram why both a catalyst and heating increase rate. For the catalyst, they should:
toLevel4.answer: draw a second Ea line to the left of the original, on the same curve
distractors: draw a second curve shifted to the right of the original
draw a second curve shifted to the left of the original
erase the original Ea line and draw nothing in its place

toLevel4.stem: On the same diagram, for the temperature increase the student should:
toLevel4.answer: draw a second curve that is shorter, broader, and shifted right
distractors: draw a second Ea line to the left of the original
draw a second curve that is taller, narrower, and shifted left
increase the total area under the original curve

toLevel4.stem: A student draws a combined diagram correctly. They notice the shaded area beyond the catalysed Ea line is larger than the shaded area beyond the uncatalysed Ea line for both curves. What does this confirm?
toLevel4.answer: A catalyst increases the proportion of particles able to react regardless of temperature
distractors: A catalyst only works at one specific temperature and has no effect at others
The catalyst has changed the shape of the distribution curve as well
The uncatalysed reaction has a lower Ea than the catalysed reaction

toLevel4.stem: A student examines a combined diagram and observes that the greatest proportion of reactive particles occurs when both a catalyst is used and temperature is increased. Why?
toLevel4.answer: The curve shifts right (more high-energy particles) and Ea moves left (lower threshold) — both effects combine
distractors: Using both a catalyst and temperature cancels out their individual effects
The catalyst raises the temperature automatically, doubling the effect
Temperature moves the Ea line further left than the catalyst alone

toLevel4.stem: A student is asked to label the area on a combined diagram that represents particles able to react ONLY because of the temperature increase (not the catalyst). Where is this area?
toLevel4.answer: The area beyond the uncatalysed Ea that is under the high-temperature curve but not under the low-temperature curve
distractors: The area between the two Ea lines under the low-temperature curve
The entire area under the high-temperature curve from zero to infinity
The area to the left of both Ea lines under the low-temperature curve

toLevel4.stem: On a combined diagram, the temperature effect is shown by a second {{blank:1}}, while the catalyst effect is shown by a second {{blank:2}} line.
distractors: Ea
curve
axis
peak

toLevel4.stem: The greatest proportion of reactive particles occurs when both effects combine: the curve shifts {{blank:1}} and the Ea line moves {{blank:2}}.
distractors: left
right
up
down

toLevel4.stem: The area between the two Ea lines under the original curve represents particles that can react only because of the {{blank:1}}, not because of a {{blank:2}} increase.
distractors: temperature
catalyst
pressure
concentration

toLevel5.stem: On a combined Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram, a student observes that the catalysed Ea line intersects the high-temperature curve at a point where there is a large area to the right. What does this tell us about combining both strategies?
toLevel5.answer: Together they produce the largest possible proportion of particles able to react
distractors: The effects cancel out and the proportion stays the same as the original
Only the catalyst is effective; the temperature increase has no additional benefit
Only the temperature is effective; the catalyst has no additional benefit

toLevel5.stem: A student draws a combined diagram but makes the high-temperature curve with a larger total area than the low-temperature curve. What error have they made?
toLevel5.answer: The total area under both curves must be equal because the number of particles is unchanged
distractors: The high-temperature curve should always have a larger area than the low-temperature one
The error is in the Ea lines, not in the curve areas at all
The low-temperature curve should have a larger area than the high-temperature one

toLevel5.stem: A combined diagram shows that at low temperature with a catalyst, the proportion of particles exceeding the catalysed Ea is similar to the proportion exceeding the uncatalysed Ea at high temperature. What does this comparison suggest?
toLevel5.answer: A catalyst at low temperature can achieve a similar rate increase to heating without a catalyst
distractors: The catalyst has no effect and only temperature matters for rate
Temperature has no effect and only the catalyst matters for rate
Both strategies must always be used together to have any effect

toLevel5.stem: A peer claims: 'On a combined diagram, you can see that a catalyst always has a greater effect on rate than a temperature increase.' Is this valid?
toLevel5.answer: Not necessarily — the relative effect depends on the magnitude of the Ea reduction versus the temperature change
distractors: Yes — catalysts always produce a larger shaded area than temperature increases
Yes — moving the Ea line always has a bigger effect than shifting the curve
No — temperature always has a greater effect because it changes the curve shape

toLevel5.stem: On a combined diagram, the area between the two Ea lines under the low-temperature curve is small, but under the high-temperature curve it is much larger. What does this tell us?
toLevel5.answer: The catalyst's benefit is amplified at higher temperature because more particles fall in the region between the two Ea values
distractors: The catalyst is less effective at higher temperature because the curve is flatter
The catalyst only works at low temperature and has no effect at high temperature
The catalyst reduces Ea more at higher temperature than at lower temperature

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that showing both effects on one diagram is unnecessary because they can be understood separately. Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: A combined diagram reveals how the effects interact, which separate diagrams cannot show as clearly
distractors: The student is correct — separate diagrams always provide more information
The student is correct — combined diagrams are too complex to interpret
A combined diagram hides important details about each individual effect

toLevel5.stem: At a given temperature, adding a catalyst shifts the Ea from 80 to 50 kJ mol⁻¹. Raising temperature by 20°C would shift the curve so that the proportion exceeding 80 kJ mol⁻¹ doubles. Which strategy results in the greater rate increase?
toLevel5.answer: This depends on the specific distribution — shifting Ea by 30 kJ mol⁻¹ often has a larger effect than doubling the proportion
distractors: The temperature increase always has a larger effect than any catalyst
Both strategies always produce exactly the same rate increase
The catalyst always has a smaller effect than any temperature change

toLevel5.stem: A student draws a combined diagram with the catalysed Ea line to the RIGHT of the uncatalysed Ea line. What fundamental error did they make?
toLevel5.answer: A catalyst lowers Ea, so the catalysed Ea line must be to the LEFT of the uncatalysed one
distractors: The diagram is correct because catalysts raise the activation energy barrier
The error is that both Ea lines should be in exactly the same position
The error is that the Ea lines should not appear on the diagram at all

distractors: reduced
curve
eliminated

toLevel5.stem: A combined diagram is more informative than separate diagrams because it reveals how the {{blank:1}} and {{blank:2}} effects interact with each other.
